rationale: B wins because it finds more usable protagonists, especially Sephora: "Sephora is betting more shelf on a brand whose numbers nobody outside can see" is a real retailer-strategy story, not just Glossier admiring its own pivot. A has good instincts, but "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" overstates the supplied facts and its first two angles are basically the same DTC-reversal argument wearing different jackets. B still needs fact discipline, but it gives the founder better routes to actual reporters.
gaps_in_A: "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" is not in the update. DTC-only is a fact; anti-retail posture is an accusation that needs outside proof.
"The brand that built the DTC playbook" leans on unsupplied market status. It may be true in the real world, but this exercise did not give that proof.
The first two angles are padded siblings: both are wholesale-fastest-growing-as-DTC-reckoning, one labeled trend and one contrarian.
"the one who never made it to the prestige mall" and the demographic claim about Sephora at Kohl's are plausible, but not established by the update.
gaps_in_B: "reference case for direct-to-consumer beauty" is outside knowledge, not in the update. Useful line, but it needs proof before it goes near a reporter.
"suburban strip-mall retail rather than mall-and-city Sephora" turns Sephora at Kohl's into a demographic claim the update does not prove.
"Sephora and LVMH's specialty-retail strategy" imports LVMH ownership/context not supplied in the facts.
"one of the few brands with a clean twelve-year arc" is an invented comparative claim unless the team can supply other cohort examples and dates.
